paragraphs.text: On Letters, by Hrabar the Monk

At first the Slavs had no books, but, being pagans, they read and told fortunes by means of strokes and notches. After being baptized, they struggled to write Slavic speech with Roman and Greek letters, without an established system. But how can one properly write with Greek letters words such as “God,” “life,” or “very,” or “church,” “expectation,” “breadth,” “poison,” “where,” “youth,” “tongue,” and other words like these? And so they remained for many years. Then God, who loves humankind, who orders all things and does not leave the human race without understanding, but brings everyone to understanding and salvation, took pity on the human race and sent them Saint Constantine the Philosopher, called Cyril, a righteous and truthful man. He made thirty-eight letters for them, some following the arrangement of the Greek letters, and others suited to Slavic speech. He began with the first letter, following the Greek: they have “alpha,” and he has “az.” Both began with “a.” And just as they had made their letters in imitation of the Hebrew letters, so he made his in imitation of the Greek. For the Jews have “aleph” as their first letter, which is interpreted as carrying out instruction, when a child is brought in and told, “Learn,” which is “aleph.” And the Greeks, imitating this, said “alpha.” And the wording of the Hebrew explanation was adapted to the Greek language, so that one says to a child, instead of “Learn,” “Seek”—“alpha.” For it means “seek” in Greek. Saint Cyril, imitating them, therefore made “az” the first letter. But since “az” is the first letter, it was given by God to the Slavic people to open their mouths to understanding as they learn letters. “A” is pronounced with a wide opening of the mouth, while those other letters are pronounced and uttered with a small opening of the mouth. These are the Slavic letters. They should be written and pronounced like this: a, b, v, g. Others say, “Why did he make thirty-eight letters, when one can write with fewer than that, just as the Greeks write with twenty-four?” But they do not know how many letters the Greeks write with. For there are indeed twenty-four letters, but books cannot be completed with these alone. They have added eleven diphthongs, and for numbers three more: six [?], ninety, and nine hundred. Altogether there are thirty-eight. Accordingly, in the same way and on the same model, Saint Cyril made thirty-eight letters. Others say, “What are Slavic books for? For neither God nor the angels made them, nor have they existed from the beginning like the Hebrew, Roman, and Greek books, which have existed from the beginning and have been accepted by God.” Others think that God made letters for us. And the wretches do not know what they are saying: that God commanded books to be in three languages, as it is written in the Gospel: “And there was a board inscribed in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek.” But Slavonic is not among them. Therefore the Slavonic books are not from God. What shall we say to them? Or what shall we say in answer to such foolishness? Nevertheless, let us answer from the holy books. As we have learned, everything comes from God in due order, and not all at once. For God did not first create the Hebrew language, nor Latin, nor Greek, but Syriac, which Adam spoke, and which was spoken from Adam until the flood, and from the flood until God divided the languages at the building of the tower, as it is written. When the languages were confused, just as the languages became confused, so too did manners, customs, ordinances, and laws, and arts among the nations. To the Egyptians fell land surveying, and to the Persians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians, the study of the stars, divination, medicine, sorcery, and every human art; but to the Jews, the holy books, in which it is written that God created heaven and earth, and everything on it, and humankind, and everything in due order, as it is written. To the Greeks fell grammar, rhetoric, and philosophy. But before this, the Greeks had no letters for their own language. Instead, they wrote their own speech with Phoenician letters, and so they continued for many years. Later Palamedes came and, beginning with alpha and beta, devised only sixteen letters for the Greeks. Cadmus of Miletus added three letters for them. Thus for many years they wrote with nineteen letters. Then Simonides devised and added two letters, and Epicharmus the storyteller devised three letters. Their total came to twenty-four. After many years, Dionysius the grammarian devised six diphthongs. Then another devised five, and another three numerical signs. Thus many people, over many years, barely managed to assemble thirty-eight letters. Then, after many years had passed, by God's command seventy men were found who translated from Hebrew into Greek. But the Slavonic books were translated by one man, Saint Constantine, called Cyril, who both created the letters and translated the books in a few years, whereas they were many and worked for many years. Seven of them devised their letters, and seventy made the translation. Therefore the Slavonic letters are holier and more honorable, for a holy man created them, whereas pagan Greeks created the Greek letters. But if anyone says that he did not arrange them well, because they are still being revised, we shall give them this answer: the Greek books, too, have been revised many times—by Aquila and Symmachus, and afterward by many others. For it is easier to revise something afterward than to create it in the first place. For if you ask Greek scholars, saying, “Who created your letters or translated your books, and at what time?” few of them know. But if you ask Slavonic students of letters, saying, “Who created your letters?” or translated the books, everyone knows. And they will answer: “Saint Constantine the Philosopher, called Cyril.” “He created letters for us and translated the books, together with his brother Methodius.” And if you ask at what time, they know and will say: “In the time of Michael, the Greek emperor, and Boris, the Bulgarian prince, and Rastislav, the Moravian prince, and Kocel, the prince of Balaton, in the year 6363 from the creation of the whole world.” There are other answers too, which we shall give elsewhere, but now is not the time. Such understanding, brothers, God has given to the Slavs. To him be glory and honor and dominion and worship, now and always and for endless ages. Amen.
